title: MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows
text:
In the wake of  the Make America Healthy Again movement's midterm wipeout , a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But  a Stat report  on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place. 
 The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates. 
 The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a  $100 million fundraiser  to  boost MAHA's clout in the midterms . In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.   Read full article

title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
text:
In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. 
 Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. 
 The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.   Read full article

title: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains
text:
Blue Origin  announced Thursday  that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company's Project Suncatcher program. 
 Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers  about a year ago  and characterized the project as one of its research "moonshots." The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy. 
 "Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit," said Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. "This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what's possible for the future of compute."   Read full article

title: "You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask
text:
Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it's worth looking at how they handle climate change. 
 But there’s no  direct  way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A  study  led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer. 
 CO 2  Q&A 
 LLM research often faces ( no-true-Scotsman-tinged ) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list  in the report .)   Read full article

title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
text:
NASA  recently announced  a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon. 
 The moves were designed to give the agency's lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit. 
 These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.   Read full article

title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
text:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a  Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. 
 Across just four consecutive business days, a  mass Microsoft exchange outage  broke IT services  for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration  tech screw-up   grounded airplanes  across the country, a  software problem  affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a  United Airlines system glitch  delayed flights yet again, and an  NSA classified network’s downtime  left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a  US war with Iran  and rising fears of  AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. 
 Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack. title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
text:
In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump's pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation. 
 Late Tuesday evening,  Axios  reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of  Heidi Overton  to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy's decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats. 
 In her confirmation hearing in September,  Overton consistently stonewalled senators  on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA's current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn't say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is "quite lethal" or that children are given vaccine doses the "size of a soda bottle." Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.   Read full article

title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
text:
Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the  Office-in-Copilot overhaul  with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls  Hardened Server Core . Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the  Defense Information Systems Agency's  (DISA)  Security Technical Implementation Guide  (STIG). 
 STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened.  "   
 The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the  Server Core  installs.  Windows Server Desktop Experience  installs do not include the changed stance.   Read full article

title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
text:
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings. 
 After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it " shameful " and a " national embarrassment ." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently  over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for  over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week. 
 But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.   Read full article

title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
text:
The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity ,  The Sims ) since  the underwhelming release of  Spore  in 2008  and Wright's  subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories. 
  MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency  put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world. 
 “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?"   Read full article

title: Transatlantic securitisation gap revisited: comparing EU and US securitisation architectures
text: This paper revisits the transatlantic gap in securitisation issuance. In comparing the securitisation frameworks in the European Union (EU) and United States, we adopt a granular approach, distinguishing between instrument types and considering the broader funding and risk transfer frameworks in which securitisation operates. We conclude that the apparent gap in terms of scale stems from methodological and structural differences in how securitisation is defined and measured across jurisdictions, rather than from a structurally weaker or less developed EU securitisation market. In particular, commonly cited comparisons of securitisation volumes often exclude covered bond issuance, despite covered bonds being a significant and longstanding component of asset-backed funding in the EU. As a result, measures of the transatlantic “securitisation gap” that focus solely on conventional securitisation may overstate the difference between EU and US market-based funding. When covered bond issuance is incorporated into the analysis, a more disaggregated picture emerges: over the past two decades, asset-backed funding activity has not been structurally one-sided but has instead exhibited shifting patterns over time, reflecting differences in market conditions and positions in the financial cycle. We introduce the concept of an asset mobilisation ratio to scale issuance by the size of each economy. From this perspective, transatlantic convergence appears to be ongoing, with the gap in issuance narrowing over time, although a meaningful difference in market scale remains. However, the persistence of this gap should not be viewed as evidence that the EU market is structurally underdeveloped relative to the US market. Direct quantitative comparisons are complicated by significant differences in market structures, funding channels, legal frameworks and institutional arrangements across jurisdictions. [...]

title: Financial stability risks from large IPOs, equity issuance and passive investing
text: A new wave of equity issuance, concentrated in AI-related sectors, has brought public equity financing back to the forefront of capital markets. SpaceX’s record initial public offering (IPO) has led the way, with OpenAI and Anthropic planning to follow. This special feature assesses the financial stability implications of large IPOs and equity issuance in general, as well as how these interact with the trend towards passive investing. Primary equity financing supports financial stability by absorbing losses and limiting leverage at the firm level, but aggregate equity issuance is highly cyclical and strongly influenced by investor sentiment. Issuance peaks have historically been associated with late-cycle exuberance and weaker future returns, while equity funding tends to dry up in downturns when the ability to recapitalise matters most. The rise of passive investing is increasing the relatively inelastic demand for equities, leading to larger equity offerings and making equity financing conditions more dependent on investor flows. Although these developments do not currently constitute a systemic financial stability risk, they could amplify market cyclicality and the sensitivity of equity financing to changes in sentiment.

title: Financial stability implications of AI adoption in the financial industry and the real economy
text: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the financial industry as well as the broader economy, creating both opportunities and risks. Banks and asset managers, which represent key channels of financial intermediation in the euro area, are increasingly using AI for tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection and portfolio management. While AI adoption can support innovation and enhance operational efficiency, it may also introduce new risks and amplify existing vulnerabilities, including a reliance on a small number of technology providers that creates concentration and third-party dependencies across the financial system. At the same time, financial institutions are also increasingly exposed to AI-driven developments in the real economy. A novel firm-level indicator suggests that a sizeable share of firms, concentrated mainly in the IT and financial sectors, is significantly exposed to AI-related opportunities and risks. Policies should focus on improving the quality of data that monitor the use of AI, strengthening the oversight of critical AI providers and adapting market safeguards and supervisory capabilities to emerging risks.

title: Financial Stability Review, November 2026
Monetary policy, segmented capital markets and innovation
text: We identify a novel mechanism linking monetary policy, innovation, and capital-market segmentation. When capital markets are imperfectly integrated, contractionary monetary policy tightens the financing constraints of externally financed firms, amplifying the decline in innovation induced by tighter financial conditions; monetary easing operates in reverse. Using granular euro-area firm-level data on balance sheets and patenting, matched with bank-level and credit-registry information, we show that monetary policy affects innovation through financing constraints. The effects are strongest for firms with high intangible intensity and for firms operating in AI-related sectors. Financing structure is central: firms that rely heavily on bank credit experience larger declines in patenting following monetary tightening, whereas firms with diversified access to external finance, particularly equity, are substantially less affected. Capital-market segmentation thus amplifies and prolongs the effects of monetary policy on innovation. Greater financial integration can broaden firms’ financing options, reduce their reliance on bank credit, and thereby attenuate this amplification mechanism.

title: Decoding the cyber-AI nexus
text: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the cyber threat landscape, with significant implications for financial stability in the euro area. This special feature explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity, highlighting how advanced AI models are enabling attackers and defenders alike to enhance their capabilities. Highly capable and agentic AI systems are increasing the scale, speed and sophistication of attacks while also introducing new vulnerabilities. These include AI models themselves being exposed to novel types of attack and AI agents failing to act as their human operators intend. Critically, new AI capabilities could favour attackers, as the availability of low-cost AI agents lowers entry barriers. Meanwhile defenders remain constrained by the cost of deploying frontier models, governance challenges and slower, regulation-bound decision-making. This leaves defenders structurally disadvantaged, at least in the near term. Euro area banks, despite their high level of cybersecurity maturity, face asymmetries in access to cutting-edge AI models and rely heavily on concentrated third-party providers. This increases the risk of systemic disruption, as AI adoption transforms the channels through which cyber incidents propagate. Mitigating these risks requires banks, AI developers, cybersecurity firms and regulators to coordinate their efforts to enhance resilience, improve governance and address emerging systemic vulnerabilities.

title: The impact of monetary policy on productivity
text: This occasional paper extends previous analyses by the WGF Expert Group on Productivity of the impact of monetary policy on productivity by exploring new interactions, particularly the influence of market power and the role of productivity in the transmission of monetary policy through the banking system. Using a consistent definition of monetary policy shocks throughout the report and several large-scale micro distribution exercises across euro area countries, our study examines the short-run procyclical effects of monetary policy shocks on productivity through investment decisions. The results reveal a positive relationship between market power and the transmission of monetary policy to productivity, highlighting the role of heterogeneous markups. Our study confirms the positive impact of expansionary monetary policy on capital reallocation but finds more nuanced results for labour reallocation. It further extends the analysis to the evolution of zombie firms, revealing opposing effects of monetary policy on their entry and exit, while also exploring the interaction between bank characteristics and productivity, though the results remain inconclusive. Overall, the findings suggest that expansionary monetary policy shocks enhance productivity by improving resource allocation. However, they also raise concerns about the potential adverse effects of current contractionary monetary policy shocks on productivity.

title: The macroeconomic effects of defence spending: what impact beyond GDP?
text: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specification, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier. Capital expenditure drives the positive output effects, whereas personnel and intermediate consumption generate stronger inflationary pressures per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital spending induces additional recurrent costs, standing at about 30 cents per euro spent over five years. Multipliers are also found to be substantially lower, on average, in high public debt regimes.

title: Economic Bulletin Issue 7, 2026
Artificial intelligence and European firms: the cost of market-based financing
text: This box examines how exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) is reflected in the market-based financing conditions of European firms. Using a novel firm-level measure of AI exposure derived from the earnings call transcripts of STOXX Europe 600 constituents, we show that AI exposure extends beyond a narrow set of infrastructure providers and hyperscalers, encompassing a broader range of firms that adopt AI for product innovation or productivity gains. Panel regressions show that AI-exposed firms earn a robust equity return premium of around 1.3 percentage points per quarter and pay significantly lower option-adjusted spreads on their corporate bonds, while also issuing a relatively higher share of long-dated debt. These patterns indicate that AI exposure is priced into both equity and corporate bond markets across the wider economy in Europe and is more broadly distributed than the concentrated market rally would imply.

title: What share of public services employment is contributed by the private sector?
text: This box examines the composition of “public services” employment in the euro area. This sector has contributed disproportionately to aggregate employment growth in recent years. Drawing on the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and Eurostat’s EU Labour Force Survey, we show that only around half of the 6.9 million public services jobs created since 2008 can be attributed to the public sector. Within public services, health and social work is the dominant driver, yet this is also the least “publicly provided” sub-sector. Within health and social work, growth is concentrated in activities related to care of the elderly and disabled, which is closely linked to ageing demographics and in large part provided from outside the public sector.

title: Narratives and risks: a quantitative toolkit to evaluate scenarios applied to the Middle East conflict
text: This box introduces a new quantitative methodology to evaluate alternative scenarios around the Eurosystem/ECB staff baseline projections, with a focus on their empirical plausibility. In a first step, the methodology constructs joint predictive distributions capturing temporal and cross-variable dynamics for euro area real GDP growth and HICP inflation. It then assesses the empirical plausibility of scenario outcomes by computing the likelihood of each scenario relative to that of the baseline against historical patterns. Applied to the Middle East scenarios in the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections, the framework shows a higher empirical plausibility for the milder scenario relative to the alternative scenarios. The box highlights that the proposed empirical plausibility index goes beyond a simple assessment of scenario severity, underscoring the necessity of accounting for both temporal and cross-variable correlations.

title: Who holds stablecoins? New evidence on euro area consumer holdings
text: This box looks at whether stablecoins are on the rise in the euro area and what the implications are for financial stability, using data from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey. It highlights the transactional nature of stablecoins and the risks posed by an increase in consumer holdings. While current exposures remain limited, the analysis underscores the importance of monitoring the use of stablecoins and the potential spillover effects on consumer confidence and financial markets.

title: The real and financial effects of local corporate tax increases: evidence from linked firm–bank data
text: We study how local corporate tax increases affect firms’ financing and real activity. In Portugal, municipalities independently set a surtax on corporate income, generating plausibly exogenous variation across space and time. We link the universe of corporate balance sheets and profit-and-loss statements to loan-level data from the Bank of Portugal’s credit registry, allowing us to track firms’ liquidity, leverage, borrowing costs, and credit quality alongside revenues, employment, and productivity. We estimate local-projection difference-in-differences models that address staggered treatment timing and dynamic responses. Surtax hikes immediately tighten financing conditions: liquidity falls, implicit interest rates rise, debt increases at shorter maturities, and non-performing loans become more prevalent. These strains spill over into real outcomes: firms reduce sales and employment and experience persistent declines in total factor productivity. Effects are strongest among small firms, where leverage rises in response to liquidity losses. We also find higher exit and relocation probabilities, but no gains in neighboring output, pointing to inefficient reallocation. Our results highlight how local tax policy can transmit through both financial and real margins, with implications for fiscal design in decentralized settings.

title: The role of refining costs and margins in HICP energy inflation
text: Energy market developments continue to be shaped by the conflict in the Middle East. Global refinery runs have fallen significantly compared to previous years, driven by reduced refinery activity in the Middle East, Russia and Asia. The constrained supply of crude oil and refined products has led to a persistent global increase in refining margins and costs, particularly for diesel. In view of the important role of refining costs and margins in transport and heating fuel inflation, the ECB’s short-term inflation projection model for energy shows that expected heightened trajectories for refined energy product prices may lead to higher energy inflation even if oil prices move in the opposite direction.

title: Bill Ackman is asking the wrong question about Nvidia
text:
When an executive leaves suddenly, people watch to see whose calls still get returned. If they believe the old boss might be back in the foreseeable future, they have a reason to wait him out. At  Nvidia , where Jensen Huang famously had dozens of direct reports, that ambiguity could reach deep into the business. Bill Ackman thinks Nvidia’s board made a mistake by saying it does not intend to reinstate Huang. I think that statement was one of the more defensible things the board did. 



 Ackman’s criticism of the original decision deserves a hearing. On Nov. 8, Nvidia announced an independent inquiry and expressed confidence in Huang. On Nov. 11, according to its SEC filing, the board accepted his resignation, effective immediately, and announced his departure the next day. Ackman argues that the directors moved too quickly. Chairman Harvey Jones says Huang resigned voluntarily after disclosing conduct inconsistent with company standards. The board has offered shareholders limited detail about what changed. The speed warrants scrutiny, although the public timeline alone cannot tell us what the directors knew or when they learned it. 



 But the question of whether the board handled Huang’s departure properly is different from the question of what should happen next. Once he was out, the directors could give interim CEO Colette Kress clear authority or leave employees, customers and prospective successors wondering whether Huang would soon return. Ackman sees the board’s rejection of reinstatement as another failure. A serious and highly qualified candidate for the permanent job might see it as a reason to accept the assignment. 



 When I ran large subsidiaries of major corporations, I would have found it impossible to imagine managing anything close to 60 direct reports.  Bloomberg  reported roughly that number at Nvidia. Huang’s extraordinary span gave him direct information and influence across the enterprise. Nvidia’s achievements offer a powerful defense of his approach, but they also reveal a succession problem. Access to one exceptional founder by so many direct reports is not an organizational structure that can easily be handed to someone else. Executives accustomed to relying on Huang for decisions almost certainly had fewer opportunities to exercise independent judgment. 



 The strongest case for Huang is not sentimental. He helped build one of the most consequential companies in modern technology, and his strategic and technical instincts may be unusually difficult to replace. But irreplaceability is a dangerous principle on which to govern a public corporation. The talents that made him an extraordinary founder do not necessarily make him the right leader during a prolonged investigation, legal uncertainty and a wholesale transition in authority. 



 Kress, who remains chief financial officer while serving as interim CEO, must keep the company moving. The permanent successor will face a different task: determining where authority belongs and making the new arrangement durable. I would allow roughly a year after that person takes charge before judging the transition. Reporting lines can change overnight; confidence in independent decision-making, customer relationships and accountability cannot. 



 Meanwhile, there is a practical reason to keep Huang away from day-to-day operations. A shareholder derivative lawsuit has named him alongside numerous directors and executives. Investigations and possible additional legal proceedings create uncertainty about the demands on his time; no one can responsibly predict their ultimate scope or outcome. But even intermittent diversions could be consequential at a company whose decision-making has depended so heavily on one person. An adverse finding after reinstatement could force a second abrupt transition. Berkeley law professor Stavros Gadinis has warned that reinstating Huang before the investigation concludes could expose directors to fiduciary risk. 



 Nvidia is not a distressed company desperately searching for a rescuer. On Nov. 17, it reported quarterly revenue of approximately $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure. Strong results do not prove the transition will succeed: most of that performance reflects work undertaken before Huang’s departure. They do, however, underscore what is at stake. The board’s task is to protect an exceptionally successful business from a leadership struggle that could unsettle it. Jones has reiterated that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company has engaged Heidrick & Struggles to help find a permanent CEO. 



 That stance need not mean throwing away Huang’s expertise forever. If the investigations end favorably, and if the new CEO wants his help, Huang might advise on a particular technical question or customer relationship under clearly defined terms. A board role or limited consulting arrangement might eventually be considered, subject to governance and conflict concerns. Even a return as CEO need not be metaphysically impossible if a successor fails and the circumstances change. But none of those possibilities should become a standing invitation to undermine the person now in charge. 



 Consider the alternative: a year after the permanent CEO arrives, Nvidia continues to prosper. Customers remain loyal, the leadership team has earned confidence, and executives are making decisions within their own authority. Bringing Huang back then could have more downside than upside, reviving uncertainty and displacing a system that had proved itself. If the transition falters, the board will retain options. What it cannot afford is to deny a successor the opportunity to succeed in the first place. 



 The board cannot undo the uncertainty surrounding Huang’s departure. But it can prevent that uncertainty from paralyzing Nvidia’s future. Giving a successor the authority to succeed, while preserving the option of drawing on Huang’s extraordinary talents later, is not a repudiation of his legacy. It may be the best way to protect it.

title: How VCs are celebrating Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO
text: Today was the day we’ve all been waiting for. Anthropic silenced the critics, at least for now. It's looking like one of the best venture outcomes ever, even though the biggest winners aren’t VCs.   How do you celebrate a multibillion-dollar return?     Brendan McDermid/Reuters     Hello.  It’s Ben Bergman.  Bessemer’s Byron Deeter, Lightspeed’s Ravi Mhatre, and Menlo’s Matt Murphy were all at the Nasdaq today to ring in Anthropic’s wildly successful IPO. They each minted their firms billions of dollars on paper, some of the biggest VC gains in history. And what will they do to celebrate tonight? Wing it.    “Believe it or not, we’re in New York, and we don’t have a reservation yet,” Murphy told me when we caught up on a brief phone call between his TV appearances and meetings with limited partners. “It’s a little bit ad hoc.”   After today, they can certainly afford to slip the maître d some cash to score a table. Which one do you think will pick up the dinner tab?    Anthropic’s biggest winners are not VCs     but Amazon, Google, and its seven cofounders. Anthropic’s Series B funding round was infamously led by FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is now serving a 25-year prison sentence and would have been sitting on more than $40 billion.  Nonetheless, Anthropic’s valuation has soared to such heights that it still ranks among the best, if not the best, venture outcomes of all time. Aside from the aforementioned trio, Iconiq, GIC, Coatue, Sequoia, Spark, and Founders Fund are among the firms that made billions.      Joe Ciolli/BI    With such a long list of VCs who can brag about being early in Anthropic (even if they got in very late), it was a day of extreme FOMO for those   who never invested   or gave up the chance at a billion dollars   because of their ex  .  As for the VC trio, Murphy said they plan to eat some steak and enjoy a few glasses of wine before heading to the Morgan Stanley party, one of several banks that are celebrating tonight. He said Anthropic itself is not hosting a public celebration.   “A lot of the team is worn out from the IPO and headed back to their families and their jobs,” he said. “There's more recursive intelligence to be built, apparently.”   Read more    The buzz    Nvidia founder Jensen Huang Lisi Niesner/Reuters; BI     Katie here.  It’s hard to believe that the Anthropic IPO was almost overshadowed by another AI industry event, but the drama around Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia diverted a lot of industry attention. Most VCs I spoke to seem broadly   in favor of Huang's return,   given their general support for transformative founders. He also played a major role in the ecosystem by investing in and acquiring AI startups.   Yet Huang has an uphill battle, with ongoing investigations into his alleged misconduct with a possible spy. The board also   maintains   that Huang will not be offered his job back. However, there’s one caveat. Huang has the power to add two new board members. It remains to be seen whether he will proceed with that option and if that will be enough to tip the balance in his favor. This drama feels far from over.    Post of the week  There’s something poetic about rain in Silicon Valley on the eve of a massive liquidity event. 🌧️💰  — Adam Nash (@adamnash),   November 18, 2026  .   Around the cap table   Anthropic's IPO is set to make its cofounders, execs, and backers extremely rich.   Here's who stands to gain the most.    Serena Williams is   partnering   with longtime investor Beth Ferreira to launch a new VC firm, Starfire Ventures.   Nvidia is   telling   the robotics startups it has invested in that it still has their backs.  Palo Alto Networks   agreed to buy   Applied Compute for $4.5 billion.     The VC Insider team   Ben Bergman, chief correspondent, in Los Angeles. Katie Roof, editor at large, in San Francisco. title: Neural Network-Based Modeling of Hysteretic Systems: From Prandtl and Preisach Neural Networks to Neuro-Madelung and Neuroplastic Continuous Models
text:
arXiv:2611.23240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hysteresis is a complex nonlinear phenomenon characterized by memory dependence, path dependence, and, in many physical systems, degradation, non-congruency, asymmetry, and rate dependence. This review examines the development and capabilities of Prandtl neural networks (PNNs), Preisach neural networks (PreisachNNs), generalized Prandtl neural networks (GPNNs), the neuro-Madelung model (NMM), extended Preisach neural networks (EPNNs), and dynamic plastic continuous neural networks (DPCNNs). Particular attention is given to their mechanisms for representing memory, network architectures, activation functions, training algorithms, treatment of deterioration and rate dependence, and applications to nonlinear structural and material systems. The PNN introduced hysteretic memory directly into neural activation through stop operators and demonstrated accurate nonlinear dynamic analysis of structures. Preisach-NNs subsequently extended this concept through an additional nonlinear hidden layer to represent non-Masing hysteresis. GPNNs introduced deteriorating-stop neurons to capture stiffness and strength degradation and non-congruent hysteresis. A different generalization was provided by the NMM, which combined Madelung's hysteresis rules with multilayer feedforward neural networks to represent diverse rate-independent and rate-dependent behaviors. These developments culminated in the EPNN, which combines deteriorating hysteretic operators, nonlinear neural mappings, and input-rate information to accommodate Masing and nonMasing, symmetric and asymmetric, congruent and noncongruent, and rate-independent and rate-dependent hysteresis.

title: GridForge: An Open Physics-Informed Digital Twin and Benchmark Suite for UK 11 kV Underground Distribution Cables
text:
arXiv:2611.23241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The UK distribution-cable monitoring sector is data-rich but framework-poor: each Distribution Network Operator (DNO) collects megabytes of telemetry per asset per day, but there is no public benchmark dataset, no shared reference model, and no commonly agreed evaluation protocol for benchmarking sectoral, data-intensive models for operational decision support; notably for maintenance planning and prioritisation. We address this gap with GridForge, an open-source physics-informed digital twin and benchmark suite for fault diagnosis and prediction, integrating four building blocks: (i) a verified steady state and transient thermal model based on IEC 60287 and IEC 60853; (ii) a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables (covering 320 cable-years) representing four canonical UK 11 kV thermal archetypes and four condition modes; (iii) a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate that satisfies the algebraic balance defined by IEC 60287 during training and reaches an RMSE of 0.148 {\deg}C on an independent held out set against the reference analytical oracle; and (iv) a five-task benchmark suite that includes three reference baseline models (pure physics, gradient-boosted trees, and the PINN). All numerical parameters are sourced from public standards, the code is licensed under the MIT licence, and the trained PINN converges in only two minutes (as run on the computing platform in Section 10.1), enabling independent verification by DNO engineering and research practitioners. At present only the virtual-sensor task (T4) discriminates between the reference baselines; the other tasks tie or are undefined on this test split, so extending the baselines with task-specific logic is a priority future enhancement. For open validation, the dataset, test sets and models are made available at https://github.com/mlily2024/Gridforge

title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
text:
arXiv:2611.23242v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.

title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
text:
arXiv:2611.23244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
text:
arXiv:2611.23245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
text:
arXiv:2611.23246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.

title: Budgeted Proper Loss Design for Uncertain Decision Thresholds
text:
arXiv:2611.23247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A binary probability estimate may be used by several decision makers with different error costs. Proper scoring rules can emphasize selected probability thresholds, but a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. We study the choice of a proper loss when the threshold distribution belongs to a finite specified family. Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and a fixed total mass, we derive the weight that minimizes the sharp, distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret. The solution clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the prescribed floor; its normalization is found by a one-dimensional root search. We give proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, as well as a limitation for atomic threshold laws. An exact histogram implementation and two synthetic experiments across 20 seeds verify the construction. The optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, while fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly. The result is a loss-design guarantee under an explicit budget, rather than a general claim of predictive superiority.

title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
text:
arXiv:2611.23248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
text:
arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
text:
arXiv:2611.23324v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
text:
arXiv:2611.23339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
text:
arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
text:
arXiv:2611.23345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
text:
arXiv:2611.23358v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
text:
arXiv:2611.23359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
text:
arXiv:2611.23362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
text:
arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
text:
arXiv:2611.23375v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
text:
arXiv:2611.23386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
text:
arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
text:
arXiv:2611.23397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
text:
arXiv:2611.23398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
text:
arXiv:2611.23403v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
text:
arXiv:2611.23410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve Update
text:
arXiv:2611.23414v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

title: OCLDA-GS: Object-Centric Local Deformation-Aware Gaussian Streaming
text:
arXiv:2611.23416v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for online reconstruction of dynamic scenes from multi-view videos for Free Viewpoint Video (FVV). Current time and storage efficient methods rely on selecting a subset of anchor Gaussians and neighborhood interpolation for fast streamable 3DGS. However, these methods can overlook object-specific motion and introduce inconsistencies near object boundaries. We propose OCLDA-GS, an object-centric streaming framework that dynamically reallocates object and motion-aware Gaussian anchors to allocate anchor Gaussian support for objects undergoing large motion while at the same time, restricting the gaussian neighborhood within object groups for more precise object boundaries. Furthermore, it estimates object-wise rigid transformations (e.g. a hand moving) and leverages these estimates to learn per-anchor local deformation correction for small deformations (e.g. wrinkles on a shirt). Then, we conduct experiments on three dynamic multi-view video datasets and demonstrate improvements over the previous baselines alongside improved quality between refinement timesteps. Under matched refinement budgets, our method improves PSNR over Instant Gaussian Stream (IGS) by 0.169 dB on N3DV, 0.202 dB on Meeting Room and +0.199 on Google Immersive, while reducing the mean PSNR drop between refinement timesteps by 9.2% and 13.8% in N3DV and Meeting Room, respectively.

title: Autoregressive View Model
text:
