At each student-generated prefix, TrustMOPD measures this displacement in next-token preferences, calibrates its magnitude across teachers, and uses the resulting scores as proxies for local reliability to weight teacher-specific distillation losses. Evaluated across mathematics, code, and instruction following, TrustMOPD closes 91.5\% and 98.0\% of the overall-score gap between the initial student and oracle-routed teachers when trained on \textsc{SingleCap} and \textsc{MultiCap}, respectively, compared with 54.4\% and 54.5\% for the strongest label-free baseline in each setting. On \textsc{SingleCap}, it approaches label-based MOPD without using domain labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunjie279/TrustMOPD-.

title: WorkWorlds: Evaluating Agents in a Company Built Before the Task
text:
arXiv:2609.23806v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many knowledge work benchmarks are built around single tasks, where the context and files for each task are selected concurrently or after task definition. Research has argued that this construction method does not reflect real workplace work, yet the impact has never been measured under controlled conditions. To compare the two constructions under controlled conditions, we introduce WorkWorlds, an infrastructure that modularizes company components into revision, date, and employee seat to be separately adjusted. Using historical data donated by a real company, we reconstructed a pharmaceutical company, PharmaCo. Two experts with over ten years of industry experience each wrote eight tasks based on real events that occurred at the company, and each independently constructed a task-specific environment for every task. Across 192 controlled evaluations, when the agent was switched from the task-specific environment to all the materials truly visible to the employee, evidence access dropped from 90.4 percent to 72.8 percent, and the criterion pass rate dropped from 76.7 percent to 68.0 percent. However, in cases where the agent found the required evidence, the pass rates under both conditions were almost identical. Furthermore, switching between the environments built by the two experts for the same task resulted in an average pass rate difference of 6.6 percentage points. The three agents also gained by different amounts, which changed the gaps between them. We argue that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder.

title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
text:
arXiv:2609.26105v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

title: When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
text:
arXiv:2609.27917v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. A 2-opt local search, however, removes most of the gap at negligible cost, after which reallocation adds a few hundredths of a percent of tour length.

title: Cost-Efficient LLM Evaluation: A Framework for Narrow Confidence Intervals Under Fixed Budgets
text:
arXiv:2609.29140v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly important role in both academic research and industry. Reliable evaluation helps researchers understand model capabilities and assess progress during model development. However, evaluation can be costly, and researchers often need to assess performance within a fixed budget. Because model outputs can vary across runs, this budget must be allocated between testing different tasks and repeating selected tasks. A confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty in the resulting performance estimate. Obtaining narrower intervals at the same confidence level and evaluation cost provides a more precise assessment of model performance, helping researchers draw clearer conclusions from limited observations. We introduce a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage. The framework then uses disagreements between runs on the same task to bound estimation error, allowing narrower confidence intervals at the same confidence level when the sampled repeats show little variability. When repeated runs on each task yield the same outcome, we prove that our framework achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow. We establish matching lower bounds both when every task must be covered and when tasks may be skipped, even for evaluators who use earlier results to decide which run to carry out next. On LiveCodeBench, our framework yielded narrower confidence intervals on average than uniform random sampling in 15 of 16 model configurations, with a median width reduction of 30.6% at the same confidence level and the same budget of 1,100 outputs per configuration.

title: Rethinking the Reconstruction-Generation Gap in Representation Autoencoders
text:
arXiv:2609.31620v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fusing shallower encoder layers into a Representation Autoencoder (RAE) sharpens pixel reconstruction but degrades diffusion generation. Prior studies and the research community commonly attribute this trade-off to the latent content itself, assuming detail-rich features are harder to model. We show that this gap stems from geometric mismatch at the encoder-decoder interface. Freezing a foundation encoder preserves rich visual information, but imposes an encoder-native Euclidean metric shaped without pixel decoding, whereas the decoder amplifies sampling errors sharply along sensitive directions. At fixed information, reducing pixel error admits two dual geometric interventions: regularizing the decoder to flatten its sensitivity to latent variations, and aligning diffusion coordinates with the frozen decoder's metric at identical clean reconstruction. On ImageNet-256, aligning diffusion coordinates largely closes the guided generation penalty of multi-layer fusion and reaches state-of-the-art 0.984 gFID and 2.14 FDr6 in 80 epochs. RAEs should take information from the encoder and geometry from the decoder.

title: Elastic Selective Spectral Hybrids for Train-Once, Export-Many Budgeted Inference
text:
arXiv:2609.32486v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deploying a language model under different computing and latency budgets calls for compact models with different quality-cost trade-offs. Towards this end, elastic spectral state space models provide ordered and temporally decomposed channels that can be truncated, but they are associated with linear time-invariant filters that cannot selectively preserve relevant past information or forget irrelevant information as the context evolves. To address this, we introduce the Elastic Selective Spectral Hybrid (ESSH), which realizes each Hankel spectral channel as an independent recurrent unit using fitted damped rotation modes. It also features an input-dependent decay and write/read gates that make temporal retention and state update input-dependent while preserving channel-wise truncation and a structured recurrence for efficient execution. ESSH combines these selective spectral mixers with sliding-window attention and jointly trains multiple capacities by reducing spectral-channel count and feed-forward width at different rates through a two-rate capacity map with full-model distillation. The resulting models support chunked parallel training and fused recurrent decoding while avoiding computation for discarded channels. At full capacity, ESSH achieves language-modeling quality comparable to similarly sized independently trained models, while smaller exports exhibit a smooth quality-cost trade-off. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework using language understanding, retrieval, cross-domain text, and DNA experiments, by assessing quality retention and the trade-off against independently trained and elastic baselines. At the 1.53B model configuration, fused batch-one decoding takes 1.37 ms per token on a B300, providing a 2.14-2.80x speedup over the tested Mamba-2 and Mamba-3 implementations and 3.03x over Transformer++ at matched parameter counts.

title: Difficulty-Aware Statistical Matching for Dataset Distillation
text:
arXiv:2609.34299v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) condenses a large original set into a small distilled set with high training utility. Decoupled statistical matching methods substantially reduce distillation time and memory overhead while achieving strong performance. However, they typically supervise all distilled data with running statistics estimated from the entire original set. These statistics mainly capture the average feature distribution while ignoring the difficulty differences among original data, making them insufficient for characterizing the difficulty structure of the original data. To address this issue, we propose Difficulty-aware Statistical Matching (DSM) for Dataset Distillation. After pretraining, DSM uses the Global Difficulty Score (GDS) to evaluate image difficulty, sorts the original data according to the scores, and then partitions it into IPC (Images per Class of distilled data) difficulty groups. During distillation, Statistics Updated Again (SUA) updates the teacher's BN running statistics using original data from each group via forward passes, providing difficulty-specific supervision for each corresponding distilled batch. Meanwhile, Initial Sample Screening (ISS) initializes distilled data with original images from the corresponding group, providing an effective starting point for precise matching. Experiments across multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of DSM, showing that it broadens the difficulty range of distilled samples and further improves the final performance. Code will be released.

title: SANTA++: Sampling Attention through Representative Keys
text:
arXiv:2609.35629v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Attention often concentrates on a small subset of tokens in the context, but which subset matters changes from one query to the next. To exploit this changing structure, we introduce SANTA++, a training-free stochastic attention method that uses representative keys for memory-efficient selection without scanning the entire key-value (KV) cache. Cached keys are organized into teams, and the query scores one representative from each team to decide which teams to sample. We compute exact attention scores within the sampled teams and reweight each team's contribution by the inverse of its inclusion probability. This importance sampling correction estimates attention over the full cache, with a sampling budget that lets us trade memory reads for accuracy. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at 32K context, contiguous SANTA++ at S=1024 retains 95-98% of dense aggregate scores on LongBench v2, HELMET RAG, and RULER using 28-31% logical KV access. On RULER, SANTA++ outperforms Quest across the tested accuracy-access sweep, using 48.7% fewer KV reads at approximately 79% accuracy. It also outperforms MagicPIG at low access. At S=1024, our Triton implementation gives a 1.38x attention-operator speedup over the Flash backend of PyTorch scaled dot-product attention (Flash SDPA) in FP16. At batch eight, full-model decoding is 1.23x faster than dense Flash SDPA with matched INT4 model weights and FP16 KV-cache precision on an RTX 5090 Laptop GPU. Our kernels are available at https://github.com/OPUSLab/santapp-kernel-demo.

title: Reimagine Video Dynamics: A Unified Framework for Video Editing with Editable Spatiotemporal Tokens
text:
arXiv:2609.36496v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most video editing methods can change how a scene looks but offer limited control over how it moves. We introduce Reimagine Video Dynamics (RVD), a unified framework for editing actions, motion pace, and appearance with reusable dynamics tokens and a shared renderer. The tokens capture motion from the source video and retain an explicit temporal axis. A language-guided editor transforms them to change an action or event. Resampling them changes the pace of motion, while keeping them fixed allows the renderer to reproduce the motion with a new appearance. We train the renderer to reconstruct source videos. We pretrain the editor on motion from real videos, then fine-tune it on counterfactual pairs. Across 450 dynamics edits, RVD achieves the highest instruction-following score and an 80.0\% pass rate. The same renderer supports retiming and motion reuse without additional task-specific training.

title: Masked Swingers: Harnessing Data Augmentation to Advance Autoencoders for Self-Supervised Learning
text:
arXiv:2609.38278v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) trains on inputs alone, allowing us to make models that are more useful in more settings. The autoencoder SSL framework learns by reconstructing its own input after information loss through a bottleneck or noise injection. Masked autoencoders (MAE) are the most successful instantiation of this framework: they encode a random subset of patches, then decode the masked-out patches. In this work, we introduce key modifications to improve MAEs. Our method augments an image in two different ways, then masks and encodes each view separately. It then exchanges the global representations (CLS tokens) between views before decoding the masked patches. By design, our Masked Swingers encourages learning a view-agnostic summary of the image for efficient transfer. We perform extensive experiments, and find Masked Swingers outperforms the official MAE checkpoint by +10.7% averaged over 10 frozen-feature tasks at equal pre-training compute. Gains are highest on fine-grained tasks, e.g., instance retrieval. Swingers also reduces error by 64% relative to MAE on three new state-probing datasets for world modeling, while keeping the fine-tunability of MAE. Post-training by swinging nearest neighbors gains again, e.g., by +5% on IN-1K kNN, opening the door to learning invariances via autoencoding.

title: No Corners Cut: State-Grounded Transitions for Mid-Stream Prompt Switches in Video Generation
text:
arXiv:2609.38691v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Streaming video generators allow users to dynamically modulate video synthesis via mid-stream prompt switching. Existing streaming methods can respond to the updated instruction while still cutting corners, prematurely realizing goals or taking heuristic shortcuts that bypass necessary intermediate state changes needed for a plausible transition. In this study, we present SEGUE, a novel framework that makes this process explicit and trains the generator to execute these transitions faithfully. At each switch, a training-free planner parses the latest frame and prompts, writes a few segue prompts with roles and durations, and then hands control back to the user's prompt. Furthermore, to address the inherent difficulty of training causal models on short-lived temporal schedules without corrupting preparatory supervision, we introduce SpanDMD, which evaluates each active prompt using the full rollout as temporal context while retaining its DMD residual only within the prompt's assigned span. On OpenTrans-360, a benchmark of 1,800 switches that scores how the old state exits and the new one begins, SEGUE ranks first on all eight transition metrics and raises the overall score over the strongest baseline from 0.866 to 0.887. It leads on four of six StreamAV-Bench instruction-response metrics and achieves the highest CLIP score in all five post-switch segments of VBench-Long evaluation, while the planner transfers to frozen autoregressive generators without retraining.

title: Risk-Calibrated Intent Routing for Conversational AI via Signed Lexical Evidence
text:
arXiv:2610.00262v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Conversational AI has become widely used as advances in language models let people find information, get writing help, and ask for practical guidance in their own words. When an assistant handles specific tasks, it must infer what the user wants and decide whether to act on that prediction. A sentence classifier's confidence can miss clues in the wording. We combine the gap between the classifier's two highest scores with signed lexical evidence, a score based on words and short character patterns. The score is positive when those patterns favor the predicted intent and negative when they favor another. We use separate calibration data and a statistical upper bound on the error rate to set the minimum confidence required to accept a request. Across ten runs per dataset, our method reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve, which summarizes error as more requests are accepted, by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, respectively, compared with a confidence model that uses only sentence classifier scores. At a 5% error target, the share of accepted requests rises by 1.83 percentage points on BANKING77 and 5.14 points on HWU64. CLINC150 already has near-full coverage at that target. At a 2% target, calibration finds a rule that accepts some requests in all 30 runs. Our contribution is a two-feature confidence model that improves routing by measuring how strongly the wording supports or challenges the original intent prediction.

title: IQS-BO: In-Context Query Selection for Bayesian Optimisation
text:
arXiv:2610.01269v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Bayesian Optimisation (BO) is a powerful framework for optimising expensive black-box functions, but typically requires refitting a surrogate and maximising an acquisition function at every evaluation. In-context approaches based on Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs) amortise part of this cost by pre-training transformers on functions drawn from synthetic priors. PFNS4BO amortises the surrogate but still relies on a numerically maximised acquisition function, while FIBO performs BO fully in-context by sampling optimiser locations from a learned density, which fixes the decision rule and admits no surrogate. Learned acquisition functions score a finite candidate set with a network, but, lacking a label for the query, learn the score by reinforcement learning. We propose IQS-BO, a PFN that learns the query decision by supervised learning on synthetic priors. In a single forward pass, IQS-BO predicts the probability that each candidate is the best in the set, and we show that training minimises its expected KL divergence to the posterior probability of this event. The model can be pre-trained without a surrogate for fully in-context BO, or take the predictions of a fixed probabilistic surrogate as additional input, amortising only the decision step. Our method proposes queries at a fraction of the cost of acquisition-based methods, while matching or outperforming BO with Gaussian processes (GPs) and available in-context methods in sequential and batch optimisation, in low and high dimensions. Finally, we propose a mixture prior for pre-training PFNs which combines samples from GPs with functions exhibiting warped inputs, narrow optima, or plateaus that are poorly modelled by stationary GP kernels. We show that pre-training on this prior can improve performance and help the network generalise to a broader range of optimisation problems.

title: When Is Accuracy Evidence? A Unified Theory of Generalisation, Validation, and Information Fusion
text:
arXiv:2610.03465v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: K-fold cross-validation (CV) is widely used as evidence of out-of-sample performance, although folds are neither independent experiments nor equally informative under heterogeneous data. Cross Upper-Bound Validation (CUBV) replaces point-wise CV accuracy by conservative upper bounds on true risk. Here we generalise CUBV through a single exponential framework in which the moment-generating function of the generalisation gap is controlled by a cumulant envelope gamma(lambda). This yields a family of risk bounds covering Hoeffding-, Bernstein-, dependency-aware, PAC-Bayesian, and heterogeneous source-fusion settings. For K-fold CV, dependence between fold-wise gaps is modelled through a joint sub-Gaussian proxy matrix. Under equicorrelation, this gives an effective number of folds, Keff = K/[1+(K-1)rho], showing that increasing K does not necessarily increase statistical evidence when folds are strongly dependent. The framework is also extended to posterior distributions over predictors and weighted multi-source fusion, where weights are selected by minimising an upper bound on future risk rather than empirical error alone. Experiments with trained linear classifiers on heterogeneous multimodal Gaussian mixtures compare K-fold CV with full-sample resubstitution plus risk correction. Bounds are evaluated by coverage and tightness. In low-dimensional small-sample settings, K-fold partitioning can increase uncertainty because individual folds under-represent minority modes, while corrected resubstitution can remain valid and tighter; this effect disappears as sample size increases. Overall, gamma-CUBV separates observed performance, uncertainty, dependence, model complexity, and confidence into explicit terms, providing a unified route from CV scores to risk statements and a principled validation criterion for heterogeneous small-sample applications such as neuroimaging.

title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
text:
arXiv:2610.04433v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A coding agent is a language model inside a harness: the system prompt, the tools, and the context management that let a chat model work in a repository. Most of the engineering on these agents goes into the harness, and vendors and leaderboards credit it with score gains. Earlier studies have fixed the model and swapped the harness, but have not measured whether the swap changes the pass rate more than running the same harness again. We run seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged. No harness leads consistently across models. Where the data can bound the difference between two harnesses, the bound is 2 to 5 points, and a harness swap changes about as many task outcomes as a rerun. The exceptions are harness effects in particular pairings of model and harness, whose direction changes with the model: OpenCode trails by 8 to 9 points on one model and leads by 14 on another. Cost differences between harnesses also depend on the model, from under 10% to 3 to 4 times. Which harness is better therefore has no answer apart from the model, and a harness difference should be reported next to a rerun.

title: DV-Lens: Revealing the Functional Organization of Language Model Parameters
text:
arXiv:2610.04489v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Understanding parameter functions helps elucidate the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to connect parameters from different modules to verifiable output effects and further characterize the relationship between their functional organization and model capability remains to be explored. To this end, we introduce the downstream vocabulary lens (DV-Lens), a parameter-level interpretability framework that links native parameter directions to their downstream vocabulary responses. Specifically, we first estimate module-specific downstream Jacobians over a reference prompt set for attention query, key, value, and output (Q/K/V/O) projections and feed-forward networks (FFNs). Second, we use these mappings to project native parameter columns into the final vocabulary space, obtaining signed readouts that characterize their average local output responses. Third, we group parameter columns by their vocabulary readouts and introduce downstream vocabulary complexity (DV-Complexity), which quantifies within-group structural variation using normalized reconstruction residuals of the original weights. At the parameter level, randomized controls and finite-difference tests show that DV-Lens readouts capture non-random vocabulary structure and predict local logit changes with 98.0% coordinate-orientation agreement across 720 cases from nine models. These readouts further guide parameter ablation, steering, and swapping across 21 models, shifting target-token probabilities in the predicted directions under controlled conditions. At the model level, the joint-parameter score of DV-Complexity achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.904 with benchmark-based capability rankings across 48 language models. Together, these results provide intervention-based evidence for DV-Lens interpretations and reveal an association between DV-Complexity and model capability.

title: Think Before You Distill: Generalization Recovery in Quantized VLAs via Selective Policy Distillation
text:
arXiv:2610.05745v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Post-training quantization has been shown to preserve VLA performance under standard evaluation conditions, but whether it preserves the full-precision model's robustness and generalization remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically study the robustness and generalization of post-quantized VLA policies under environmental disturbances. Empirical results show that quantized policies can become fragile to subtle environmental variations despite retaining comparable in-distribution performance. We further observe that action discrepancies are concentrated in a small subset of the rollout states, while teacher guidance has opposite effects depending on discrepancy: it improves performance at high-discrepancy states but can degrade it at low-discrepancy states. These findings reveal that effective post-quantization recovery requires selective intervention on vulnerable states rather than globally distilling the student. We therefore propose Policy-Induced Vulnerability-Oriented Tuning (PIVOT-Q), a vulnerability-aware On-Policy Distillation (OPD) framework that selectively corrects vulnerable states encountered during quantized-student rollouts using the frozen full-precision policy as a teacher. PIVOT-Q identifies vulnerable states using discounted accumulated discrepancies over a short horizon, applies phase-balanced sparse supervision, and uses a Behavioral Anchor to prevent unintended changes. Experiments under seven LIBERO-Plus environmental variations demonstrate consistent recovery across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods. Notably, PIVOT-Q outperforms full-state distillation with smaller variance across evaluated settings while using only 20\% of its state-level distillation budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruanruan-andy/PIVOT-Q.

title: Coordinate-Free Corridor Reconstruction and Field-of-View Framing Attribution for 3D Bilateral Coronary Artery Trees in CT Angiography
text:
arXiv:2610.05900v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Bilateral coronary tree extraction from cardiac computed tomography angiography (CCTA) must transfer from cropped benchmarks to uncropped scans without territory swaps or lattice staircases. Using 35 training scans, we fix a coordinate-free three-dimensional network (597,032 parameters) and a flush-admissible 8.0 mm corridor solver refined by a learned medial offset. We evaluate once on 50 ImageCAS scans against Lee94 thinning skeletons and zero-shot on 40 ASOCA scans (20 healthy, 20 diseased; 80 trees) against Vascular Modeling Toolkit (VMTK) Voronoi consensus centerlines. On uncropped pericardial ASOCA scans, our method leads all comparators on per-artery Chamfer distance (6.90 mm automatic despite 14.22 mm ostium error; 7.05 vs. 9.11 mm seeded, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.0047$). It also leads 1 mm centerline F1 (51.42% and 51.56%, +13.21 to +29.08 percentage points [pp], $p_{\text{Holm}} \le 9.0 \times 10^{-4}$) at $1.66 \pm 0.07$ s/scan on an NVIDIA L4 graphics processor. In cropped ImageCAS boxes, it leads F1 (76.98%) while trailing 18--22 mm bridgers on mean distance (3.37 vs. 2.72--3.20 mm; none significant after Holm). Pitch-matched 1.19 mm zero-clutter controls show coarse pitch degrades matched U-Nets whereas fixed-frontend distance reversal requires pericardial clutter. Flush collar gating rescues 30/32 seeded ASOCA stubs (-7.97 mm), and the learned medial offset raises node (+2.72 to +5.11 pp; bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence interval [+2.42, +3.01] on ImageCAS) and curve (+1.87 to +4.40 pp) F1. Short corridors curb pericardial chaining while learned offsets lift centerlines off the lattice.

title: Considering Context: When World Models Need Context Encoders
text:
arXiv:2610.06651v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Methods for generalization in model-based reinforcement learning typically assume that an agent cannot recover the latent context governing the environment dynamics from its own experience, and therefore supplies it externally. We formalize and test this assumption with \emph{predictive sufficiency}, which quantifies what access to the context adds to next-step prediction under the visitation distribution an agent induces, and separates that quantity into a history-recoverable part and a residual requiring the true context, both distinct from a finite model's deficit. We classify context-aware algorithms by the predictive risk their conditioning set can target and demonstrate across environments of increasing identification difficulty that the headroom does not follow the MDP class. The same task under different priors leaves predictive headroom in one setting and nothing distinguishable from zero in another, where the agent's behavior implicitly identifies the context and any benefit of such a mechanism cannot be attributed to missing one-step predictive information. Where headroom persists, the learned state exposes it only partially, and adding the true context still lowers the risk. Our contribution is an analytical framework, instantiated by a practical criterion for matching contextual mechanisms to the predictive information available to them, estimated from the ordinary trained agent.

title: CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use
text:
arXiv:2610.09127v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

title: An Invariant Tangent-Angle Descriptor and a Band U-Net for 2D Fragment Adjacency Prediction
text:
arXiv:2610.09459v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reassembling a broken artefact begins with deciding which fragments are adjacent. This paper addresses adjacency prediction for pairs of 2D fragments by analysing their contours. We propose a two-stage pipeline. In the first stage, each contour point is encoded using a tangent-angle profile, a descriptor that does not depend on rotation, translation or the choice of starting point. Pairs of profiles are then used to build an adjacency matrix, each entry computed either from a log-likelihood ratio or using a small 1D convolutional network. In the second stage, a U-Net classifies this matrix to predict whether the two fragments are adjacent. We compared our pipeline with two approaches from the literature using their own datasets. The results show that our approach outperforms them by reaching a Recall@10 of 0.823 versus 0.564 on the real dataset of PairingNet, and an accuracy of 0.979 versus 0.916 on Beaulac's dataset.

title: Scenes as an Attack Surface: Uncovering Scene-Grounded Safety Failures in MLLMs
text:
arXiv:2610.14094v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Existing jailbreak attacks have exposed serious safety weaknesses in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Most prior attacks rely on specially constructed visual inputs to carry or support harmful intent. In this paper, we uncover a different vulnerability: task-relevant scene semantics alone can shift an MLLM from refusal to compliance, even when the visual input introduces no additional attack instructions and the original task intent remains unchanged. We formalize this failure as a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability and introduce SceneSafetyBench to investigate it across eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs. Our analysis reveals that this failure is associated with how task-relevant visual evidence influences downstream safety representations, suggesting that visual grounding alone cannot fully explain the observed safety shift. Building on this finding, we propose Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task while constructing validated scene-grounded queries and combining their independent responses. Across nine target MLLMs, SGA achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 86.17%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models. Our results identify scene semantics as an overlooked attack surface in MLLMs and highlight a growing tension between stronger visual grounding and robust multimodal safety alignment.

title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
text:
arXiv:2610.14226v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Objectives: Radiologists interpreting oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT must also detect non-oncologic conditions, yet existing CT foundation models are trained on single anatomical regions or on non-oncologic data. We developed and evaluated CAPTOR, a vision-language foundation model for oncologic CAP CT that uses an anatomically structured preprocessing strategy to learn from whole examinations.
  Materials & Methods: CAPTOR is a contrastive vision-language model pretrained on 25,512 predominantly oncologic CAP CT-report pairs (single or multiple series) from a retrospective multicenter dataset (North America, Europe, Asia). It was compared with five CT foundation models, a larger-scale variant (CAPTOR-100K) and an ablation without anatomical preprocessing (CAPTOR-NoPre) on classification and retrieval using held-out internal and public test sets, and on survival prediction using TumorImagingBench. Confidence intervals and pairwise comparisons used patient-level bootstrap and permutation tests.
  Results: On 10,794 test studies, CAPTOR achieved higher AUC than all five models on CAP (0.767 vs. 0.695 for the next-best model; p<0.001) and oncologic subsets (0.784 vs. 0.734; p<0.001), with superior retrieval on both, and ranked first on three of four oncologic survival benchmarks. Despite substantially fewer training examinations, it performed comparably to CAPTOR-100K. Removing the anatomically structured preprocessing reduced classification performance, including on the institutionally held-out test subset (macro-AUC 0.737 vs. 0.691 for CAPTOR-NoPre, p<0.01).
  Conclusion: Anatomically structured preprocessing enabled whole-examination CAP CT interpretation, including multiple-series acquisitions, and improved downstream performance. CAPTOR outperformed state-of-the-art CT foundation models on CAP and oncologic subsets while matching a substantially larger-scale variant.

title: MemeLogos: Knowledge-Driven Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Harmful Meme Detection
text:
arXiv:2610.15463v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: With the rapid proliferation of social media, harmful memes have become a growing threat to online ecosystems. Their harmfulness is often implicitly conveyed through complex interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, making accurate detection challenging. Recent studies have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and external knowledge into harmful meme detection. However, existing methods mainly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary information, limiting their ability to capture reusable harmfulness knowledge and underlying reasoning mechanisms, and thus constraining both detection performance and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose MemeLogos, a knowledge-driven retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for harmful meme detection. MemeLogos abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into reusable knowledge units and organizes them into a dedicated star-shaped knowledge graph. By combining structured knowledge retrieval with an explicit multi-stage reasoning process inspired by cognitive mechanisms, MemeLogos leverages retrieved knowledge to guide harmfulness reasoning, improving both detection reliability and interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemeLogos consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detection methods while generating more coherent and interpretable reasoning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured harmfulness knowledge for multimodal content understanding.

title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
text:
arXiv:2610.16352v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: One Checkpoint, Many Runs: Recipe Cards for Fine-Tuned Models
text:
arXiv:2610.16825v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fine-tuned language models are shared with model cards that describe the training setup in detail, often down to the default random seed, but report the score of a single released checkpoint. Such setups are retrained routinely, by fine-tuning services for each customer, by organizations at each update, and by users on their own data, so the model that is deployed comes from a new run of the setup. Some runs fail, and a failed run can go unnoticed and reach the people the model serves. We call such a setup a model recipe and argue that its documentation should state how often a run of the recipe misses a required performance bar. In a survey of the model cards of 300 fine-tuned language models on Hugging Face, none reports this failure probability, and only three report results from more than one training run. Across 2,124 fine-tuning runs, we find that reading the mean, the median, or a bootstrap interval as an approval often approves recipes whose failure rate exceeds a stated failure tolerance, because these summaries do not measure how often a run fails. Model cards do not report how often the runs of a recipe fail, although whoever runs the training is best placed to count them, while those who rely on a retrained model bear the cost of a failed run. To report this failure probability directly, we propose recipe cards, an addendum to model cards that documents the model recipe behind a checkpoint. A recipe card states the bar and the tolerance and who chose them, reports how many runs are made and how many of them miss the bar, gives an upper bound on the failure probability, and warns when this bound exceeds the tolerance. Recipe cards record who set and who accepted this risk, and let deployers and regulators state acceptance criteria for retrained models.

title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
text:
arXiv:2610.17895v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Shared Spatial Fields
text:
arXiv:2610.18186v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large-scale applications of lifelong multi-agent path finding (LMAPF) call for computationally inexpensive movement decisions under changing traffic conditions and across varied layouts. We propose a navigation policy in which a convolutional network computes a shared spatial field over the map once per timestep and a compact goal-conditioned operator derives agents' movement preferences. The complete policy is trained end-to-end using average-reward reinforcement learning with throughput as the reward, without planner demonstrations or a separate online path planner. For structured and unstructured layouts, we train one policy per class on pools of small maps and deploy each without retraining on larger, unseen layouts and agent populations. Across six layouts with 10,000 agents, our policies achieve throughput comparable to or higher than the strongest evaluated baselines. The proposed method has an average execution time below 10 ms per step, more than an order of magnitude faster than several established planners.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
text:
arXiv:2610.19520v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) preserve material evidence lost in RGB, yet 3D material identification from multi-view HSI faces two obstacles. Spectral Gaussian splatting reconstructs spectra accurately but leaves unmixing to per-pixel post-processing, while multi-view hyperspectral capture is costly and real datasets lack pixel-level material labels and sub-pixel proportions. We propose Spectral World Renderer (SWR), a material-aware explicit representation that unifies 3D spectral reconstruction and unmixing: it fits a Gaussian scaffold from RGB and decodes ray-Gaussian intersections into abundances over a shared endmember dictionary. Additionally, appearance guidance prevents spectrally similar materials from merging when intensity absorbs their brightness differences. Moreover, SWR requires no material-label supervision during training. To address the data gap, we further construct the SWR Benchmark (SWR-Bench): a coding-agent pipeline generates eight indoor and outdoor worlds from measured reflectance, aligning HSI with both annotations. SWR achieves the highest mIoU in all eight worlds and the highest mean PSNR on each real dataset. On an 11-class urban world, it trains at least 3.67x faster than unmixing baselines; rendering averages 34.9 joint spectral and label views/s over four worlds on a single RTX 4090.

title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
text:
arXiv:2610.23297v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

title: Typed Decision Models under Prevalence Shift and Label Budgets: Decision Training, Calibration, and Implicit Priors
text:
arXiv:2610.26325v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return probabilities over caller-defined options, and Jev's vendor describes it as calibrated. We ask whether vendor decision training improves a model over its backbone, whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift like a fine-tuned classifier's, and how many labels a trained model needs to overtake a TDM. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and trained classifiers on identical candidate-set decisions from five public datasets (on intent datasets, within the gold label's intent group) under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests frozen before the confirmatory analysis (earlier test-data checks disclosed), and estimate label-budget curves. First, decision training is not always beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment, a loss that persists across prompt formats; Tev1-4B's largest gain over its backbone is a prompt-format effect. Second, on 50 fixed moderate shifts, Jev's top-label calibration error and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, sensitive to the prior set; averaged over 2,000 shifts the gap is at most one point. Third, label-free EM correction with the model's implicit prior lowers Jev's shifted calibration error where it is highest, but labelled recalibration lowers it far more. Fourth, DeBERTa needs 100-250 labels to overtake Jev on hate speech and does not clearly overtake it on CLINC150 at any budget; a QLoRA adapter on Qwen3.5-4B overtakes Jev with at most 2,500 labels on every dataset, on CLINC150 only marginally and not under in-budget selection. The TDMs tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; their lead over trained models depends on the task.

title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
text:
arXiv:2610.26651v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
text:
arXiv:2610.26829v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: ProteinGeoBench is a set of 131 tasks that give an agent protein structure files and ask it to look up recorded facts, check sequences, calculate geometry from atom coordinates or reason about structures. We ran four frontier models on every task several times (4,249 runs) and 26 models on a subset. A single overall score hides two different skills. Three of the four frontier models are best at looking up facts and worst at calculating from coordinates: Claude Opus 5 scores 0.907 on lookup and 0.716 on calculation. Gemini 3.1 Pro is the exception. Geometry is overrepresented among the hardest tasks. Half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail are calculations, although calculations are a fifth of the suite, and eight of the twelve were solved by none of the 26 models. The three leading models are within 0.031 of one another, too close to order, and with one run per task a different model ranks first in 24% of bootstrap resamples. Reports should therefore give scores by task type and the number of runs per task. They should also state the agent harness, the software that runs the model, and its network access, because both change scores. On a 15-task subset, blocking eight structural databases lowered scores, and removing network access lowered them more. Replacing our harness with each provider's own command-line agent moved scores by up to 0.09 in either direction. Across the 26 models, those that scored higher on the other tasks also scored higher on calculation.

title: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution
text:
arXiv:2610.26924v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. DataPraxis-5K is available at huggingface.co/datasets/stargazerhust/DataPraxis-5k

title: Geometric state space, memory representation and architectures
text:
arXiv:2610.29526v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce a geometric framework for deriving attention architectures. A sequence forms a memory $m\in M_n$, and an attention pairing $\rho_n\colon M_n\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,A)$ determines how that memory acts on each token state. Different representations of this action recover familiar architectures: softmax attention reads individual key--value pairs, linear attention accumulates their contributions in matrix statistics, and Intention fits a regression map from keys to values. The framework also suggests new architectures by changing the geometry of the query--key pairing, the function carried by each value, or the space representing the memory. ImageNet-1K experiments illustrate these constructions through geometric CAFormer variants, a ViT with query-dependent values, and a linear ViT with a wider memory representation.

title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
text:
arXiv:2610.31511v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations \rev{through separate per-player decision calls}, selecting high-level actions \rev{and image-labeled target cells} while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of \rev{two-player} coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding\rev{; text gives no station coordinates, so target locations come mainly from the image}. The evaluation compares \rev{five VLMs and a privileged scripted reference policy on all 20 maps}, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, \rev{aim accuracy}, and model API expenditure. \rev{Two paired ablations on all 20 maps toggle a shared self-authored notebook and reduce the textual prompt from about 3,600 to about 440 words while keeping the images fixed.} \rev{The strongest model completes 35\% of orders and exceeds the scripted reference, which has ground-truth station access; the notebook's effect is mixed in sign and not statistically reliable, and reducing the prompt text lowers the score of two models while leaving the other three nearly unchanged.} Together, the environment design and evaluation protocol provide a framework for investigating how visual state tracking and task scheduling contribute to coordinated cooking behavior.

title: Tempo-Zero: Recursive Self-Play in Executable Worlds for Video Reasoning
text:
arXiv:2610.32433v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Video reasoning requires understanding how events unfold over time, yet videos with accurate temporal annotations are expensive to collect. Self-play offers an alternative by letting a model generate and solve its own tasks without manual annotation. However, existing video self-play methods train on fixed sets of recorded videos, so they cannot alter the underlying event dynamics and rely on noisy pseudo-labels derived from the model's own outputs, such as majority voting, that risk reinforcing shared model errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Tempo-Zero, a self-improvement framework that closes a loop of executable environments, execution-verified self-play, and environment evolution, where executing a program renders a video with the ground-truth option and interval of every question. A single policy plays both Questioner and Solver, proposing questions and answering them with timestamped evidence lines, and is trained on execution-grounded rewards instead of model consensus. The Solver's performance steers a curriculum over tasks and difficulty levels, and the policy selects rule changes that enrich the event dynamics of later rounds. Despite being trained solely on simple programs, without supervised fine-tuning or external video data which prior methods typically require, Tempo-Zero outperforms the base models and recent self-play baselines on average across twelve real-world video benchmarks at different model scales, with particularly strong gains on temporal grounding tasks. Project page: https://alchemist-jo.github.io/tempo-zero/

title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
text:
arXiv:2610.33941v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by eliminating test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, aggregating representations from all video world model layers can introduce redundant computation, while standard backpropagation may distribute action-supervision gradients unevenly across layers, limiting the effectiveness of world representation learning. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that learns to efficiently aggregate and optimize world representations for action prediction. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces an efficient world representation aggregation mechanism that restricts aggregation to a bounded range of relevant world model layers identified through layer relevance analysis. Within this bounded range, TurboWAM estimates aggregation weights for different world model layers based on the current action denoising state and combines them with learnable layer-wise weights to fuse world representations. Moreover, TurboWAM employs a world model gradient modulation mechanism that decomposes action-supervision gradients into a layer-shared component and layer-specific residual components, enabling more balanced gradient propagation across world model layers. This mechanism operates exclusively during training and introduces no additional inference computation. Together, these designs enable more efficient world representation learning and low-latency action prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks show that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: Query-Driven Learning for Lifted Reasoning
text:
arXiv:2610.34747v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Learning and reasoning are both essential to intelligent agents, but have traditionally been treated as two separate stages: first learning a knowledge base from data (or taking one as given), and then verifying queries as if the knowledge base were complete. This separation has been shown to be inefficient when the downstream goal is to verify only a small set of queries. Moreover, it neglects the possibility that data and a knowledge base contain partial yet complementary information, requiring an agent to combine both sources to justify or refute a query. Motivated by the need to integrate learning and reasoning more tightly, we study the problem of query-driven learning for reasoning. More specifically, we extend prior work to the first-order setting, which is critical for practical applications as the number of ground atoms typically grows rapidly. We begin by asking when validating or refuting a universal query given partial data and knowledge base is even possible, and identify a necessary and sufficient condition called bounded concealment. We then propose a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm that solves the task at the lifted level. Finally, we establish soundness and completeness guarantees relative to space-bounded lifted proofs, along with quasipolynomial sample and runtime bounds, demonstrating that lifted query-driven reasoning can be efficient even when unrestricted knowledge-base learning is not.

title: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Stateful Streaming Inference for Multimodal LLMs on Edge SoCs
text:
arXiv:2610.35309v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Streaming multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must take in new video frames while answering questions about what they have already seen. On an edge SoC, if one engine does both, ingestion and answering compete for its time while the other engines sit idle. To take over a query, another engine must first import or rebuild the accumulated history, because each runtime keeps it as KV state in its own format. 
ame lets one engine answer from history that another engine built. Each query reads the history as it stood when the query was asked, so one engine can keep ingesting while another answers. The CPU and GPU can also decode answers to different queries simultaneously. Phase-level state continuation lets an engine prefill a query, pass its KV state to another engine for decoding, and return to ingestion. State-Driven Execution Planning (SDEP) chooses where each query is prefilled and decoded, based on the state each engine holds and the work queued on it. Across M4 Max, RK3588, and QCS6490, 
ame outperforms single-engine execution. On a live M4 Max stream, SDEP cuts p95 time to first token by $76\%$, and every query receives its first token within one second. Under backlog, it raises request throughput by up to $35\%$. For two concurrent video streams on RK3588, SDEP delivers $19.6\%$ higher request throughput than single-engine execution and $27.2\%$ more than running both engines in parallel without shared state. 
ame delivers up to $2.48	imes$ the throughput of the same engines run serially. Every answer matches serial execution token for token.

title: FOCUS: Active Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Model Agents
text:
arXiv:2610.35801v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Sparse outcome rewards make it difficult for long-horizon language-model agents to assign credit to earlier actions. Learned critics provide value estimates for intermediate states, but these estimates can be inaccurate, while estimating intermediate values with repetitive continuation samples from points within a trajectory incurs substantial costs. To mitigate these issues, we introduce FOCUS, an RL method that uses selective branching to help the critic network learn its value estimator. The rollout controller facilitates active learning for the critic by sampling continuations from states that are expected to most reduce the critic's estimation error. These refined value estimates then score the segment between consecutive states with a TD($\lambda$) advantage, while the sampled evidence supplies training targets for the critic. FOCUS supports long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning through a modular context-management interface that decouples context management from rollout allocation. Our experiments show that using compaction-induced segment boundaries for value estimation and credit assignment, FOCUS outperforms GRPO and VinePPO with matched per-step generation budgets on legal reasoning, deep search, and code localization benchmarks, improving held-out accuracy at Qwen3.5-9B scale by 7.2 points over the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus (55.4 vs. 48.2) and by 4.1 points on DeonticBench (56.5 vs. 52.4).

title: TGTV: Interpretable Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection in UAV Telemetry
text:
arXiv:2610.38106v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Anomaly detection in multivariate fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) telemetry is complicated by operating-condition transitions, asynchronous sensor sampling, and control-system compensation that can obscure fault signatures. Existing temporal detection methods have limited capacity to represent coupled faults across subsystems, track their evolution, and constrain language-model diagnoses with quantitative evidence. This paper proposes TGTV, an interpretable framework for multivariate telemetry anomaly detection and traceable fault analysis that integrates spatiotemporal graph learning with a large language model. A temporal convolutional network and a graph attention network with weighted fused adjacency extract multiscale temporal patterns and spatial dependencies among sensors. A hybrid temporal Transformer and variational autoencoder then evaluates window-level anomalies using prediction errors and reconstruction probabilities. Continuous-time Shapley attribution identifies critical sensors and high-contribution intervals while preserving the temporal continuity of fault evolution. A structured evidence package combines detection results, graph relationships, temporal attribution, sensor attribution, and operating context. An evidence-constrained diagnosis protocol uses this package to generate flight-level conclusions with traceable evidence identifiers. Cross-flight holdout experiments on the public ALFA fixed-wing flight dataset yield a window-level area under the precision-recall curve of 0.976, accuracy of 0.973, recall of 0.902, and F1 score of 0.920. Flight-level fault diagnosis achieves recall of 0.943 and an F1 score of 0.944. These results demonstrate accurate anomaly detection and quantitatively supported fault-tracing cues, providing a basis for interpretable post-flight fault review and analysis.

title: TCC-RAG: Temporal Causal Chain-Guided RAG for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
text:
arXiv:2610.38366v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
text:
arXiv:2610.40362v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We find that the effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory accounts for most of the loss dynamics difference between WN and WD. Matching blockwise ELR trajectories step by step closely aligns their loss curves. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR). Building on this principle, we model directional-alignment dynamics under WN and derive $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay as the optimal schedule. For finite-horizon pretraining, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay) to match prescribed peak and terminal LRs. Experiments on 128B- and 500B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining under WN show that AIR outperforms cosine and alternative schedules in loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by 0.01 relative to cosine. We further identify late-stage scheduling as the primary source of this gain through controlled stage interventions, and demonstrate that a shared late schedule progressively attenuates alignment differences left by earlier LRs. Finally, transferring AIR's ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the same improved loss dynamics, demonstrating that these gains come from ELR scheduling itself and extend beyond fixed-norm training.

title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
text:
arXiv:2611.00515v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Dual-Ground-Truth Scorecard Benchmark for Smartphone Recommerce Inspection
text:
arXiv:2611.00791v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Remote smartphone recommerce is scaling quickly, and locking a repurchase offer from seller photos and diagnostic screens before the handset arrives has become a central operational task. Existing multimodal resources mainly target defect localization, catalog attributes, or screen reading. They overlook payout-facing scorecards with dual cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of a large weakly labeled trade-in corpus kept separate from a compact audited ranking cut, and (2) architectures that either flatten unordered photo bags into one prompt or collapse evaluation into a single price scalar. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth recommerce framework with PhoneValue-Corpus for weak training on 21,550 orders and 278,748 images, and PV-Rank as the only leaderboard on 335 quality-gated orders. Systems are ranked by CardScore under LeadGate, with Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill as diagnostics, while grade and price stay off the board. Notably, ValueAgent is a six-stage perception-fusion reference that canonicalizes views, detects regional defects, reads screenshots, and fuses evidence under warehouse-style rules, so bag-of-images prompting is not the only evaluation unit. On the same PV-Rank cut and frozen scorer, this full-system and input-contract comparison finds ValueAgent at 84.1 CardScore against the strongest Flat Vision-Language Model at 69.9, with the largest reported gap in CosFill, while OpsFill remains limited under the two declared contracts. CardScore measures field-fill completeness, not quote accuracy.

title: Profile-aware assessment of block-diagonal Hessian approximations in neural networks
text:
arXiv:2611.01335v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Evaluating block-diagonal curvature models in neural networks involves two questions: how much curvature they omit, and what a specific correction changes at a finite step. We measure the squared off-block fraction of the parameter Hessian against references for group sizes and the observed within-group curvature profile. In CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 and a skip-free counterpart, similar initial discarded fractions accompany different profiles. At saved trained ResNet-18 weights, changing from stage to layer groups moves estimated off-block mass from below to above the profile reference. An approximate assessment of probe uncertainty conditional on fixed weights and inputs resolves this crossing; some skip-free comparisons remain unresolved. Separately, in nine saved ResNet-50/Stanford Cars states from three training seeds, we compare candidates formed from off-group Hessian action, the remaining model residual and their combination. For each state, we construct two full-Hessian-informed maps on separate geometry draws. Within each draw, all three inputs share one map. At unit scale off-group input alone raises evaluated minibatch loss relative to the base preconditioner candidate in 17 of 18 state/draw comparisons, yet the combined candidate has lower loss than the remainder-only candidate in nine of those cases; preferences vary with scale and correction-norm matching. The profiles help assess block models and alternative groupings, while same-state candidate comparisons test a particular correction without equating structural mass with training gain.

title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3DGS World State
text:
arXiv:2611.01543v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging due to incomplete target-view guidance and inconsistencies accumulated during scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch.
